title: Explaining and Preventing Alignment Collapse in Iterative RLHF
claim: Naive iterative training drifts into exploiting a learned proxy and collapses, while our foresighted correction converges to the true optimum.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right trajectories over heatmap, faint vector-field arrows, region labels
description: A single 2-D plot with signal magnitude on the x-axis (0–5) and noise magnitude on the y-axis (0–3). The background is a green heatmap of true human utility, shown on a colorbar from 0 to 10, with darker green near the bottom right. Faint blue and red arrows show the two gradient fields. Both trajectories start at a black dot at the origin. The red RLHF path runs almost straight up and to the right and ends at a dark red X in the high-noise region. A bold dark-red label there reads 'Alignment Collapse'. The blue FPO path arcs up slightly and then curves down to a navy star next to the gold 'Human Ideal' star near the x-axis. A bold green label there reads 'Robust Alignment'. A legend box at upper left lists the markers.
caption: Simulated policy optimization in a linear toy setting. Axes separate signal and noise components of the policy's action, and the heatmap shows the true utility. The myopic gradient of standard iterative RLHF (red) leads to alignment collapse, while the FPO gradient (blue) incorporates the parameter-steering correction and converges to the human ideal. See details in Appendix [ref].
abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) typically assumes a static or non-strategic reward model (RM). In iterative deployment, however, the policy generates the data on which the RM is retrained, creating a feedback loop. Building on the Stackelberg game formulation of this interaction, we derive an analytical decomposition of the policy's true optimization gradient into a standard policy gradient and a parameter-steering term that captures the policy's influence on the RM's future parameters. We show that standard iterative RLHF, which drops this steering term entirely, suffers from alignment collapse: the policy systematically exploits the RM's blind spots, producing low-quality, high-reward outputs whose feedback reinforces the very errors it exploits. To mitigate this, we propose foresighted policy optimization (FPO), a mechanism-design intervention that restores the missing steering term by regularizing the policy's parameter-steering effect on RM updates. We instantiate FPO via a scalable first-order approximation and demonstrate that it prevents alignment collapse on both controlled environments and an LLM alignment pipeline using Llama-3.2-1B.
